strengths: The paper addresses a very important and practical problem: unsupervised discovery of instance-specific symmetry distributions and robust canonicalization of poses.

The core idea—using the Fréchet mean of relative poses in a neighborhood to align arbitrary canonical representations—is mathematically sound, elegant, and theoretically supported (with proofs in the appendix).
It overcomes a key limitation of prior class-pose decomposition methods, where arbitrary canonicals prevented using the learned canonicalization directly at test-time for frozen classifiers.

The empirical evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning 2D image benchmarks (MNIST, FashionMNIST) and, notably, large-scale 3D molecular conformations (GEOM-QM9) under SO(3) rotations, showing excellent generalization to 3D groups.

The proposed method shows practical utility in downstream tasks, specifically Out-of-Distribution (OOD) pose detection and granting group invariance to pre-trained, frozen backbones at test-time without any retraining.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality figures that make the intuition and problem formulation easy to follow.
weaknesses: The method relies on a $k$-NN approximation in the invariant latent space $\mathcal{Z}$ to define equivalence classes. If the latent space of the underlying class-pose model is poorly structured or noisy, the quality of the neighborhood will degrade, which could hurt the Fréchet mean estimation. More discussion on how the performance scales with the quality of the underlying representation would be valuable.

Although the paper identifies SGM (Allingham et al., 2024) as the most closely related work, a direct quantitative comparison with SGM in the experimental sections (e.g., Table 5 or Figure 5) is largely missing.

The robust Tukey-Fréchet mean introduces a hyperparameter $c$ (the robustness threshold). The paper would benefit from a clearer guide or heuristic on how to automatically select $c$ for arbitrary lie groups or highly diverse datasets.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important problem in class-pose disentanglement networks—the arbitrariness of the learned canonical orientation—using rigorous group-theoretic tools. The proof of convergence of the empirical Fréchet mean to the true symmetry distribution in Wasserstein distance (Proposition 3.1) is a strong theoretical contribution.

Introducing the Tukey-Fréchet mean using robust M-estimators is a clever and practical solution to address cases where the standard Fréchet mean falls in low-density regions of multimodal distributions.

The paper demonstrates the utility of the normalized symmetry distributions across diverse and useful downstream tasks, including unsupervised symmetry discovery, out-of-distribution pose detection, and test-time canonicalization.
Extending symmetry discovery from 2D images to 3D molecular conformations (GEOM-QM9) using steerable graph neural networks (SEGNN) is a non-trivial and welcome evaluation.
weaknesses: Strong Assumption of Symmetric/Unbiased Pose Distributions: The fundamental premise of using the (robust) Fréchet mean to retrieve the "natural pose" relies on the assumption that the observed poses are symmetrically distributed around the true canonical reference frame. In real-world datasets, pose distributions are often highly biased (e.g., due to viewpoint bias, gravity, etc.). If the pose distribution in the dataset is skewed, the Fréchet mean will align with the biased mean, meaning the recovered canonical representation will still be rotated/skewed relative to the true physical canonical.

Complexity and Cascading Errors of the Multi-Stage Pipeline: The proposed method requires a complex, multi-step training pipeline: (1) training an unsupervised class-pose model (IE-AE), (2) computing latent representations for all training samples, (3) running a k-nearest neighbors search to estimate the equivalence classes, (4) calculating empirical Tukey-Fréchet means on the Lie group to generate pseudo-labels, and (5) training two auxiliary networks (Theta and Lambda) using these pseudo-labels. This multi-stage process is computationally expensive and highly susceptible to error propagation. Any failure in the initial disentanglement or the k-NN class estimation will directly degrade the final predictors.

Dependence on Perfect Disentanglement and Latent Space Clustering: The accuracy of the equivalence class approximation heavily depends on the invariant encoder mapping structurally similar objects to tight, well-separated clusters in the latent space. While this might hold for simple datasets like MNIST or pre-aligned molecular conformers, for complex real-world data, unsupervised representations often suffer from class overlap. If the k-NN search retrieves neighbors of different semantic classes, the calculated Fréchet mean will be computed over a mixture of different symmetry distributions, leading to incorrect normalization.

Marginal Performance Improvements on Complex 3D Tasks: While the performance gains on rotated MNIST and FashionMNIST are notable, these are simple datasets. On the more realistic 3D geometric graphs task (GEOM-QM9), the accuracy improvement of RECON over the baseline with no canonicalization is quite marginal (55.70% vs 52.40% in Figure 6d). Given the immense complexity of training the multi-stage pipeline, including 3D message-passing networks, this small accuracy boost might not justify the overhead in practical applications.

Comparison and Baseline Selection: The comparison in the test-time canonicalization and OOD detection tasks is restricted to simple baselines like IE-AE and SGM. The paper would benefit from comparing against other established canonicalization techniques or frame-averaging baselines (such as those by Puny et al., 2022 or Kaba et al., 2023) quantitatively in the main text.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental and practical limitation of class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrariness of the learned canonical representations, which prevents direct alignment and comparison of instance-level symmetry distributions.

The theoretical framework is solid. The authors mathematically prove (Proposition 3.1) that normalizing the relative poses by the inverse Fréchet mean recovers the true target symmetry distribution centered at the identity.

The introduction of the robust Tukey-Fréchet mean is a clever and highly practical modification, ensuring that the canonical pose does not fall into low-density regions for multimodal/bimodal distributions (such as symmetric structures).

The evaluation goes beyond simple 2D toys and successfully scales symmetry discovery to 3D groups (SO(3)) using molecular conformations (GEOM-QM9) and Steerable GNNs, which is highly challenging and a first for this type of unsupervised discovery.

The downstream applications are very compelling. In particular, the test-time canonicalization serves as an elegant, retrain-free, drop-in step to grant group invariance to standard pre-trained models, showing dramatic accuracy recoveries under rotation shifts.
weaknesses: The method heavily relies on the quality of the invariant latent space Z to perform class clustering via k-NN. If the invariant features fail to cleanly separate different semantic classes/shapes, the retrieved neighbors will be noisy, leading to poor estimation of the centering transform.

The pipeline is multi-staged and relatively complex: first training an Invariant-Equivariant Autoencoder, then performing offline k-NN retrieval and Fréchet mean calculation to generate pseudo-labels, and finally training two separate invariant networks (Theta and Lambda). This adds considerable computational and engineering overhead compared to end-to-end approaches.

While the authors show robustness to the choice of the neighborhood size k around 25, this hyperparameter might still require careful tuning on larger, more imbalanced, or more complex datasets where the density in the latent space varies widely.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and unresolved challenge in class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrariness of the learned canonical reference frame, which previously prevented consistent symmetry distribution discovery.

Provides a rigorous mathematical formulation (Proposition 3.1) proving that the empirical Fréchet mean can consistently estimate and correct the arbitrary offset to recover identity-centered symmetry distributions.

Demonstrates successful scaling to complex 3D SO(3) rotational symmetries on real-world molecular conformation datasets (GEOM/QM9), whereas most existing symmetry discovery methods are limited to 2D image domains.

Shows strong capability in handling context-dependent and partial symmetries (such as distinguishing rotated '6' and '9' digits), which typically cause representation collapse in standard equivariant networks.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, featuring clear expositions, intuitive conceptual figures, and comprehensive visualizations of recovered 3D distributions on the sphere.
weaknesses: The framework's success is heavily dependent on the quality of the pre-trained class-pose model (IE-AE). If the invariant encoder fails to produce well-separated, connected clusters for structurally similar objects, the k-NN approximation of equivalence classes will degrade, subsequently harming the normalization step.
The method introduces additional computational overhead during the pseudo-label generation phase, as it requires performing a k-NN search over the entire training set in the latent space.

The current implementation of the learnable mappings ($\Theta$) relies on parametric assumptions (e.g., Gaussian, Matrix-Fisher). While effective for the evaluated setups, this limits the method's ability to model more complex, arbitrary multi-modal symmetry distributions compared to non-parametric or flow-based density estimators.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and highly relevant limitation of class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrariness of the learned canonical pose, which previously prevented comparing or aggregating symmetry distributions across different classes or instances.
Provides a solid theoretical foundation. Proposition 3.1 mathematically justifies why canonical orientation normalization works, proving Wasserstein convergence to the true symmetry distribution.

Successfully extends unsupervised instance-level symmetry discovery to 3D groups (SO(3)) on complex geometric graph data (molecular conformations in the GEOM dataset), representing a significant advancement over prior work restricted to 2D.
Demonstrates practical downstream utility through out-of-distribution (OOD) pose detection, achieving strong quantitative results (AUC-ROC).
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with highly illustrative figures (such as Figures 1, 2, and 4) that make the core concepts and motivation very easy to grasp.
weaknesses: The pipeline is multi-stage: it requires pre-training an IE-AE, performing a k-NN search over the training set to compute pseudo-labels, and then training two additional networks ($\Theta$ and $\Lambda$). This complexity makes the method dependent on the quality of the initial representation and the hyperparameter $k$.

In the discussion on 'Picking up on partial symmetries' (Section 5.1), the mechanism of separating digits '6' and '9' is slightly unclear. If the backbone IE-AE collapses '6' and '9' to the same canonical reconstruction (as shown in Figure 6b, column 2), it implies they share very similar or identical invariant representations in $\mathcal{Z}$. If so, the k-NN search would mix samples of '6' and '9', resulting in a bimodal relative pose distribution rather than separate monomodal distributions. Clarifying how the invariant space successfully separates them despite the canonical collapse would strengthen the paper.

For the 3D experiments on GEOM, the ground-truth symmetry distributions are synthetically applied matrix-Fisher distributions. While this is useful for controlled quantitative evaluation, it leaves open the question of how well the method performs on naturally occurring, highly complex, or highly asymmetric physical orientation distributions.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental, well-known limitation in unsupervised class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrary orientation of the learned canonical representations which prevents direct comparison of pose distributions.
Provides a mathematically principled framework using the Fréchet mean on Lie groups to define and normalize to a 'natural' pose, supported by a theoretical convergence proof in Wasserstein distance.

Successfully extends unsupervised instance-level symmetry discovery to 3D rotation groups (SO(3)) using molecular conformation data (GEOM), which is a significant step forward compared to existing works that are limited to 2D image benchmarks.
Demonstrates clear downstream utility, such as out-of-distribution (OOD) pose detection, with strong AUC-ROC results across multiple datasets.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written and clear, featuring intuitive figures (e.g., Figure 4 demonstrating upright digit canonicalization) and detailed implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the method essentially acts as a multi-stage post-processing wrapper around a pre-trained Invariant-Equivariant Autoencoder (IE-AE) by computing neighborhood averages and performing a right-translation.

Highly dependent on the disentanglement quality of the pre-trained invariant latent space Z. If the IE-AE's invariant representations do not cluster perfectly or if they contain residual pose information, the k-NN neighborhood approximation of the equivalence class [x] will be noisy, degrading the normalization.
The framework still requires pre-specifying the Lie group G (e.g., SO(2) or SO(3)) prior to training, rather than discovering the symmetry group itself from scratch.

The multi-step pipeline (training IE-AE, computing training-set k-NN to get pseudo-labels, and training downstream regression networks) is computationally heavy and complex to tune, as reflected by the long training times mentioned in the appendix (several days on an A100).

strengths: Addresses a fundamental limitation of class-pose disentanglement methods—namely, the arbitrary nature of the learned canonical representation—by proposing a geometrically grounded alignment method.
Formulates the centering problem elegantly using Fréchet and Tukey-Fréchet means on Lie groups, supported by a convergence proof (Proposition 3.1).
Provides a highly versatile, plug-and-play canonicalization layer that can be applied to frozen pre-trained backbones at test time without retraining.

Demonstrates strong empirical validation across diverse domains: 2D images (MNIST, FashionMNIST) and complex 3D molecular datasets (GEOM-QM9), showing benefits in both symmetry recovery, out-of-distribution (OOD) pose detection, and test-time canonicalization.
weaknesses: Highly dependent on the quality of the underlying class-pose decomposition backbone. If the invariant latent space Z fails to separate distinct classes or if the equivariant pose predictor is inaccurate, RECON's performance will be directly bottlenecked.

The class approximation relies on a k-NN search in the latent space Z. For very large or highly sparse datasets, finding a representative neighborhood might be computationally expensive or inaccurate.

A noticeable performance gap remains between test-time canonicalization and fully equivariant models in complex domains (e.g., 55.92% for RECON vs. 98.55% for SEGNN on GEOM-QM9), highlighting the limitations of test-time post-hoc canonicalization compared to built-in equivariance.

The definition of 'natural pose' via the Fréchet mean of the dataset's pose distribution implies that if the training data is highly skewed or biased, the identified 'natural' pose will inherit this bias, potentially leading to non-ideal canonical representations.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant problem in unsupervised representation learning: resolving the arbitrary orientation of canonical representations in class-pose disentanglement frameworks.

The proposed method is geometrically principled, formulating the alignment correction using the Fréchet mean on Riemannian manifolds and extending it to a robust Tukey-Fréchet mean to handle multimodal distribution profiles.
The evaluation is extended beyond typical 2D toy datasets to 3D molecular conformations under SO(3) rotations (GEOM-QM9 dataset), which is a commendable and realistic testbed.
The paper is well-written and includes extensive experimental details, runtime analyses, and sensitivity studies in the appendix.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a high-quality pre-trained backbone: RECON relies entirely on the assumption that the invariant latent space Z of the underlying class-pose model (e.g., IE-AE) is well-clustered. If there is significant class overlap (as shown in FashionMNIST in Figures 11 and 12), the k-NN neighborhood approximation degrades, which directly compromises the quality of the canonicalization.

Low absolute performance in 3D downstream tasks: For the GEOM-QM9 dataset, while RECON (55.92%) improves upon the uncanonicalized baseline (52.40%), there remains an enormous gap compared to a fully equivariant network (SEGNN, 98.55%). This raises concerns regarding the practical utility of using test-time canonicalization in 3D domains over simply training equivariant architectures.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: The core strategy—grouping samples in a latent space, computing their average pose on a Lie group, and right-multiplying by its inverse to align them—is conceptually very similar to classical Procrustes alignment or coordinate registration techniques. Applying this as a post-processing correction step on top of an autoencoder is useful but offers limited algorithmic novelty.

Sensitivity and selection of the robust threshold parameter: The robust Tukey-Fréchet mean introduces a critical hyperparameter 'c' to limit the influence of far-away modes. The paper lacks a robust discussion or sensitivity analysis on how to choose or adaptively tune 'c' in an unsupervised manner across different datasets and group structures.

strengths: Addresses a key, well-known bottleneck in class-pose decomposition methods: the arbitrary orientation of learned canonical representations, which prevents aligned, cross-class symmetry analysis.

Provides a solid theoretical foundation (Proposition 3.1) proving that right-translating relative poses by the inverse of their neighborhood's Fréchet mean asymptotically converges to the true identity-centered symmetry distribution.

Introduces the robust Tukey-Fréchet mean to successfully handle multi-modal symmetry distributions (e.g., the digit '8' or molecular symmetries), preventing the optimization from collapsing to unobserved, 'in-between' canonical poses.

Demonstrates highly practical applications, such as a drop-in test-time canonicalization layer that grants rotation-invariance to pre-trained, frozen backbones (like ResNet or GCN) without needing labels or retraining.
Validates the method thoroughly on both 2D images and complex 3D molecular graph structures (SO(3) group), showing strong results for symmetry recovery and OOD pose detection.
weaknesses: High dependency on the quality of the base model's invariant representation: If the initial class-pose model (e.g., IE-AE) fails to separate classes cleanly in the invariant latent space Z, the k-NN neighborhood approximation will mix classes and lead to noisy or incorrect Fréchet mean estimations.

Large performance gap in complex 3D scenarios: For the molecular dataset (GEOM-QM9), while test-time canonicalization with RECON outperforms other test-time methods, the final accuracy (55.92%) remains vastly inferior to a fully equivariant model (98.55%), highlighting the challenges of plug-and-play canonicalization in 3D.
